summary: The CATENATE extension extends IMAP APPEND so a client can build a new message on the server from new data plus parts or whole messages already stored there. No download and re-upload is needed. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) CATENATE extension lets a server build a message from new text and parts of messages already stored there. The client avoids downloading and uploading those parts.

subtitle: An IMAP extension that builds a new message on the server from new text plus pieces of messages already stored there.

tldr.problem: To compose a message from parts that already sit on an IMAP server, a client would otherwise have to download those parts and upload them again.
tldr.mechanism: CATENATE extends APPEND so it takes a list of message literals and IMAP URLs. The server joins all the pieces, in order, into one new message.
tldr.outcome: Resource-constrained clients save bandwidth and processing, and can archive sent mail or edit drafts without moving large attachments. The client stays responsible for valid message structure. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3501 and RFC 3502.

today: RFC 4469 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2006 and has been updated by RFC 5550. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The CATENATE extension lets an IMAP client create a message on the server that includes the text of messages, or parts of messages, that already exist there, without a FETCH and then an APPEND back.

It does this by extending the APPEND command. Instead of a single message literal, the command can take any combination of message literals and message URLs (from the IMAP URL Scheme, RFC 2192). The server takes all the pieces and catenates them into the output message. It can also coexist with the MULTIAPPEND extension to append multiple messages in a single command.
sections.plainLanguage: CATENATE lets an IMAP client assemble a new message from literals and URLs to stored messages or parts. The server appends the pieces in the order the client lists them.

sections.title: What It Is Used For
sections.content:
The motivating use case was a resource-constrained client composing a message for later submission that contains data already in its IMAP store. Because large parts are not downloaded and re-uploaded, bandwidth and processing limits matter less. The client can also archive a copy of a sent message without uploading it twice. Sending the message is outside the scope of the document.

Other uses the RFC lists: copying only the necessary parts of a message to another mailbox and then deleting the original, which frees space where server storage is limited; and adding data to a message, such as prepending header fields, by catenating new data onto a copy of the original.
sections.plainLanguage: CATENATE can save bandwidth when a client reuses stored content. It can also help archive sent mail or copy selected message parts into another mailbox.

sections.title: The Extended APPEND Command
sections.content:
A server that supports the extension lists CATENATE in its response to the CAPABILITY command. The APPEND arguments are a mailbox name, an optional flag list, an optional date/time string, and then either a single message literal or CATENATE followed by a parenthesized list of parts. The result is OK, NO (for example if data cannot be fetched) or BAD.

Each part is either TEXT with a literal, whose octets are appended, or URL with an IMAP URL, whose body part is appended as if the literal from a FETCH BODY response were put in place. Parts are appended in order. The command does not set the \Seen flag on any catenated body part and does not change the selected mailbox.

If the server also implements UIDPLUS, a successful tagged OK carries an APPENDUID response code.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends APPEND with a list of text literals and message URLs. The server copies each part in order and does not convert or validate the resulting message structure.

sections.title: URLs and What the Client Must Get Right
sections.content:
This document covers only relative IMAP URLs, those with no scheme or server part, that refer to messages or message parts on the current server in the current authenticated session. The base URL is imap://user@server/, or imap://user@server/mailbox when a mailbox is selected. No further LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE is performed. An absolute URL or anything else would need another extension, and a server implementing only this one would return NO.

The server copies octets unchanged. It does no data conversion, such as MIME transfer encodings, and does not check that the data fits the MIME part it lands in. The client is responsible for producing a valid Internet Message Format or MIME message, including MIME boundaries between body parts and Content-Type and Content-Transfer-Encoding lines where needed.
sections.plainLanguage: This extension handles relative URLs that refer to the current server and authenticated session. The client must make sure the combined content forms a valid message.

sections.title: BADURL and TOOBIG Response Codes
sections.content:
Two response codes may appear in a tagged NO when APPEND fails.

BADURL is returned when a URL cannot be processed, for example because of bad URL syntax, an unrecognized URL scheme, an invalid message UID or an invalid body part. It contains the first URL that caused the failure.

TOOBIG is returned if the resulting message would exceed the 4-GB IMAP message limit, for instance three URLs for 2-GB messages. Even without returning it, a server must defend against clients that try to build a message over that limit. It may also return TOOBIG for a server-specific size limit.
sections.plainLanguage: BADURL identifies the first URL that the server could not process. TOOBIG reports a result that exceeds the IMAP message size limit.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content: The grammar is in ABNF. It extends append-data from the collected IMAP ABNF extensions (RFC 4466), and extends capability and resp-text-code from RFC 3501. A cat-part is either TEXT and a literal, or URL and an astring that holds an IMAP URL.
sections.plainLanguage: The command grammar lists one or more parts after CATENATE. Each part is either new literal text or a URL to stored content.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says CATENATE raises no security considerations beyond those already present in the base IMAP protocol and in the use of IMAP URLs, which are discussed in the IMAP and IMAP URL documents.
sections.plainLanguage: CATENATE adds no security issues beyond IMAP and IMAP URLs. Those underlying protocol rules still apply to the client and server.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The appendix gives four examples. They show replacing an attachment in a draft without downloading it, replacing edited text and changed header fields in a draft (with the old draft marked \Deleted and an APPENDUID response), stripping an attachment and leaving a small explanatory text part in its place, and a failed command that returns BADURL while building a digest of several messages.

The last example notes that the server could have validated each URL as it was received, and returned the tagged NO with BADURL instead of sending a continuation request.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show replacing a draft attachment, updating text while retaining an attachment, removing an attachment, and reporting an invalid URL. In each case the server joins the requested parts.

data.title: CATENATE grammar
data.code:
append-data =/ "CATENATE" SP "(" cat-part *(SP cat-part) ")"

cat-part = text-literal / url

text-literal = "TEXT" SP literal

url = "URL" SP astring

resp-text-code =/ toobig-response-code / badurl-response-code

toobig-response-code = "TOOBIG"

badurl-response-code = "BADURL" SP url-resp-text

capability =/ "CATENATE"
